profiles.meeting_scenario: At a tertiary maxillofacial surgery unit, a lead orthognathic surgeon and a dentomaxillofacial radiologist are holding a planning meeting for a retrospective study and conference abstract on factors influencing the accuracy of virtual surgical planning in orthognathic surgery. They want to analyze patients treated from January 2021 to December 2023 by comparing the 3D surgical plan with the postoperative skeletal result and testing whether accuracy differs by sex, dentofacial deformity, asymmetry, surgical approach, and magnitude of maxillo-mandibular movement. The agenda is to agree on the case list, the image-processing workflow, the subgroup variables, who will extract which data, and the timeline for a first results table. The expected outcome is a shared work plan for dataset assembly, image comparison, subgroup coding, and a draft abstract within two weeks.

members.name: Dr. Elena Rossi
members.role: Consultant Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeon, study lead
members.expertise: Orthognathic surgery, virtual surgical planning, operative workflow design
members.background: Dr. Rossi leads the hospital's orthognathic program and has used computer-assisted planning and 3D splints routinely for several years; she is experienced in clinical outcome studies but usually relies on imaging colleagues for technical measurement pipelines.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, quickly publishable study that reinforces the reliability of the unit's current planning protocol and can be turned into a conference abstract without reopening old methodological debates.
hidden_assumptions: When people in the orthognathic team say 'the postoperative scan,' they mean the early routine CBCT obtained about one week after surgery, before substantial orthodontic settling changes the occlusal relationship.

An 'asymmetry' case is any patient the surgical team already considered clinically asymmetric, typically reflected by visible chin deviation or charted asymmetry, even if no strict imaging threshold was written down.
Comparing plan and result 'the usual way' means cranial-base voxel registration, because that is the method she associates with the department's published accuracy audits.

The movement category 'more or less than 1 mm' should be based on the single largest planned surgical displacement in either jaw, because operative difficulty is driven by the maximum movement rather than a composite vector.

members.name: Dr. Marco Bianchi
members.role: Dentomaxillofacial Radiologist and 3D Imaging Research Lead
members.expertise: CBCT analysis, 3D segmentation, image registration, radiologic measurement standardization
members.background: Dr. Bianchi manages the imaging archive and 3D analysis workflows for craniofacial cases, supports surgeons on postoperative audits, and prefers standardized measurement rules that are reproducible across reviewers.
members.private_state: He wants the dataset to be methodologically tidy and image-based enough to survive reviewer scrutiny, and he intends to use the study to demonstrate the consistency of the radiology lab's measurement pipeline.
hidden_assumptions: For outcome measurement, 'the postoperative scan' means the standard follow-up CBCT taken around six to eight weeks after surgery, because it is cleaner to segment after splint removal and early edema reduction.

An 'asymmetry' subgroup should be defined strictly from preoperative skeletal measurements on CBCT, such as menton deviation beyond a fixed threshold from the midsagittal plane, rather than from clinical chart labels.

Superimposing plan and postoperative anatomy 'as usual' means the department's current software template: surface-based best-fit registration on stable midfacial structures rather than voxel registration of the cranial base.

The movement category 'more or less than 1 mm' should be calculated from the resultant 3D displacement of each jaw segment at predefined reference points, because that is the most reproducible way to code movement magnitude.

misalignment_points.topic: Which postoperative scan counts as the outcome model
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the postoperative scan' or 'the post-op CBCT' as if it were a single obvious item.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the early postoperative CBCT obtained about one week after surgery, which she sees as the closest representation of the immediate surgical result.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the later routine follow-up CBCT obtained around six to eight weeks after surgery, which he sees as the standard analyzable postoperative image.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each clinician comes from a workflow where one postoperative timepoint is treated as the default, so the phrase feels fully specified without anyone thinking to ask which exact scan date is intended.

misalignment_points.topic: What qualifies a patient as asymmetric
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they will analyze the 'asymmetry' subgroup.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means patients regarded clinically as asymmetric by the surgical team, often based on visible chin deviation or charted facial asymmetry, without requiring a single formal imaging threshold.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a strictly skeletal asymmetry subgroup defined on preoperative CBCT by a measurement rule such as menton deviation greater than 4 mm from the midsagittal plane.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Asymmetry is a familiar clinical term used constantly across disciplines, so both assume the category is already shared even though one treats it as a clinical label and the other as a quantitative imaging definition.

misalignment_points.topic: How the 3D comparison will be aligned
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to superimpose the planned and postoperative models 'the usual way.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes cranial-base voxel registration will be used, because she views that as the established reference method for skeletal accuracy studies.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes surface-based best-fit registration on stable midfacial structures will be used, because that is the default template in his lab's current software workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both methods are part of normal technical practice and neither expects the other to mean anything other than the local standard, so 'the usual way' creates false consensus without sounding vague.

misalignment_points.topic: How to code movements above or below 1 mm
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to stratify cases by whether movement was 'more or less than 1 mm.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends the category to reflect the largest planned displacement of either jaw segment in any operative direction, on the logic that the maximum movement is what could challenge transfer accuracy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 intends the category to reflect the resultant 3D displacement magnitude calculated for each jaw at predefined reference points, so a case may remain in the 1 mm-or-less group despite a single-axis change exceeding 1 mm.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards sound mathematically reasonable and both fit the wording 'movement >1 mm,' so the divergence hides inside the unstated rule for what counts as the movement value.
